text.p: Mike Tyson, once the "baddest man on the planet," may have nowhere left on the planet to try to prove it after being banned from boxing Wednesday and fined $3 million for biting Evander Holyfield's ears during their world heavyweight title fight last month.

The former heavyweight champion, whose June 28 bid to reclaim his title ended in disgrace, was not present when the five-member Nevada State Athletic Commission voted unanimously to impose the maximum punishment and revoke his license to box in the state, effectively banning him from boxing in the United States.
He perhaps could fight overseas but under terms of his probation for a rape conviction, he must ask permission to travel outside the United States.
Tyson, who once dominated the sport, can apply for reinstatement in one year but if his application for a new license is denied he must wait another year to try again.
The revocation could constitute a lifetime ban.

Holyfield, on vacation in South Africa, said only "No comment" to reporters when asked his reaction. An aide said Holyfield had nothing to add to his statement when he arrived in South Africa Sunday: that as a Christian the champion had forgiven Tyson.
Tyson's lawyer, Oscar Goodman, tried to put a positive spin on the decision, which could end the controversial career of the 31-year-old fighter.
"Next year is another year. This gives him the opportunity to come back. He's still going to be young, he's still going to be strong," Goodman told reporters outside the Las Vegas City Hall.
"In a year they have to give me a hearing and ... if I have the same commission, I feel very very confident you'll see Mike Tyson fighting (again)."

The boxing ban goes into effect when the order is signed -- probably later this week -- and Tyson has 30 days in which to appeal. Goodman said he had not yet discussed an appeal. "I will have to talk to Mr. Tyson. I don't think he's going to let me do it (appeal)."
Asked if he had advised his client not to attend the hearing, Goodman said: " Absolutely. Why should he be subjected to this?"
In the title bout, Tyson twice bit champion Holyfield's ears, taking off a portion of his top right ear in the third round before he was disqualified.
Tyson at first claimed he was retaliating for being cut by a head butt, but later apologised and admitted he had "snapped." He vowed to seek psychological counselling.
Nevada Deputy Attorney General Gordon Fink told the commission before its ruling: "The events of June 28 demand the maximum penalty...suspension is a mere interruption.
"There is a fine line between sports and chaos and what happened on June 28 went beyond that."

Holyfield's lawyer, Jim Thomas, told the hearing that while the champion accepted Tyson's personal apology, "The eyes of the world are on this commission. No boxer is bigger than the sport of boxing."
Tyson's lawyers appealed to the commission for leniency, asking the members to "do the right thing" and not be swayed by a public outcry that was demanding the boxer's banishment.

"Mr. Tyson wanted to make this short and sweet and throw himself on your mercy without any legal remedies," said Goodman, who described his client as having been "a gentleman in the ring" throughout his 13-year career.
The commission heard the arguments and with hardly any discussion voted to revoke his license and fine him 10 percent of his $30 million purse. Tyson's camp will keep the rest of the money.

The commission's acting counsel, Donald Height also noted that anyone else holding a Nevada state boxing license would be barred from having dealings with Tyson. Afterwards, commission member Jim Nave said he did not know if such sanctions would apply to Tyson's co-managers or Don King, the promoter of the Tyson-Holyfield fight.
Commission chairman Elias Ghanem told reporters: "I think what we did was the right thing. We wanted to send a message that we will not tolerate this kind of behaviour in Nevada."

Under new federal laws, a suspension in Nevada effectively bars Tyson from fighting anywhere in the United States. The law does not force other states to honour a Nevada ban, but those states would have to justify in writing allowing him to fight.
A Nevada commission member said before the decision it was his understanding that Japan would follow the panel's lead.

"I understand that Japan has talked to us and they would follow our lead but other countries have not done so as yet so I think that Mr. Tyson could fight (in other countries)", Luther Mack said in a television interview.
Tyson's career has already been shortened by the three years he spent in jail after being convicted of raping a 19-year-old beauty queen.
